questions.q: How heavy is the Saturn V at liftoff, and how much stronger is its thrust than its weight?
questions.do: Click Saturn V (Apollo) and read Mass at liftoff and Thrust over weight at liftoff under the flight chart.
questions.a: About 2,848 t, with thrust over weight of about 1.21. Thrust must be more than 1 times the weight, or the rocket cannot leave the pad.

questions.q: Compare Saturn V and ISRO’s LVM3. How much push is left in the top stage once each reaches orbit, and which targets can each reach?
questions.do: Click Saturn V (Apollo) and read Push left in the top stage and the four target boxes. Then click ISRO LVM3 and compare.
questions.a: Saturn V: about 3.10 km/s, enough for geostationary transfer and only about 0.05 km/s short of the Moon (inside the model’s error). LVM3 with its preset payload: about 1.9 km/s, only enough for low orbit, short of the Moon by about 1.2 km/s.

questions.q: What is the most LVM3 can lift to low orbit in this simulator? How does that compare with ISRO’s figure?
questions.do: Click ISRO LVM3, then click Find the most it can lift to orbit. Compare with the LVM3 row in How far to trust it.
questions.a: About 7.0 t, against ISRO’s 10 t, so the model is about 30% pessimistic. It flies one fixed pitch program and has to assume the S200 booster’s sea-level figures, while real flights steer an optimised path.

questions.q: In a blank design, change stage 1’s engine to the J-2. Why can’t the rocket leave the pad?
questions.do: Click A blank design. In Stage 1, set Engine to J-2 (Saturn V upper stages). Read the verdict and the small note under the stage. Check the Engine catalogue too.
questions.a: Thrust over weight drops to 0.00 and it “never left the pad”. The J-2 is a vacuum engine: it has no sea-level thrust (shown as — in the catalogue), so it cannot run at the ground. It was built for upper stages that light high up.

questions.q: How much did Saturn V send to the Moon for Apollo, and which Indian Moon mission did LVM3 launch?
questions.do: Read the Other rockets, published figures table, rows Saturn V and LVM3 (ISRO), and the first row of How far to trust it.
questions.a: Saturn V sent 43.5 t to the Moon. LVM3 launched Chandrayaan-3 and can send about 3 t to the Moon. With Apollo’s 43.5 t, the simulator’s Saturn V is within about 2% of the push the Moon needs.
